Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

# Clinical Vignette: Aotea M.

Aotea M. was forty-two when he came to the clinic, a Samoan electrician whose broad shoulders and weathered hands spoke of years on job sites across the city. He had been attacked three years ago, late on a Friday afternoon, in the stairwell of an apartment building where he'd been called to repair faulty wiring. A man had come up behind him—Aotea still couldn't piece together whether he'd heard footsteps or simply felt the presence—and struck him repeatedly with a crowbar. The assault lasted perhaps two minutes, though Aotea experienced it as a series of disconnected moments: the first blow to his ribs, a searing flash; his own voice shouting; the attacker's face, which he could never quite hold in his mind afterward; the weight of his own body hitting concrete. The man had fled with Aotea's wallet. Aotea had lain there, gasping, until a neighbor found him twenty minutes later.

For the first year after the assault, Aotea had pushed through. He returned to work within six weeks, told his partner Marcus that he was fine, went through the motions of recovery as though it were simply another job to be completed. But something had fractured in him that afternoon in the stairwell, and the fracture had been widening ever since. By the time he sought help, Aotea had become a prisoner of time itself. Each day at four-fifteen in the afternoon—the exact moment the attack had begun—his body would seize. His heart would race, his palms would sweat, and an overwhelming sense of unreality would wash over him, as though he were watching his own life from behind glass. He had come to dread that hour with an intensity that colored his entire week. The feeling of detachment that accompanied it was particularly unbearable; Aotea described it as being "hollowed out," present in his body but not quite inhabiting it, and this sensation would pull him back into the fractured moments of the assault itself—the snapshot of his attacker's face, the sensation of impact, the helplessness—each memory arriving not as a coherent narrative but as isolated, vivid stills that he couldn't quite connect into a whole picture. What was missing from those memories disturbed him almost as much as what remained: he couldn't remember the color of the attacker's shirt, couldn't reconstruct how long the assault had actually lasted, couldn't account for certain moments that he knew must have occurred but felt entirely absent from his mind.

When the late afternoon approached, Aotea would feel the old conviction settling into his chest: that he was fundamentally the kind of person this happened to, that someone else—someone more aware, more cautious, more worthy—would never have found himself alone in that stairwell. The guilt that accompanied his fragmented memories was suffocating; he felt ashamed of things he couldn't even fully remember, as though the gaps themselves were indictments of his character. These crushing thoughts would then amplify his sense of danger in the world. Any unexpected movement—a colleague turning suddenly on a job site, a neighbor opening a door—would trigger an adrenaline surge that left him shaking, convinced he was about to be attacked again. When Marcus would touch his shoulder without warning, Aotea would flinch violently, his nervous system interpreting the contact as a threat. He began avoiding unfamiliar places entirely, reasoning that if he couldn't assess the danger, he couldn't protect himself, a logic that felt airtight to him even as it narrowed his world. The fragments of the assault would intrude during these moments of heightened threat, each memory snapshot reinforcing his belief that he was helpless, that he had always been helpless.

To manage the approaching four-fifteen hour and the cascade of memories and fear it triggered, Aotea had developed a system of escape. He would spend hours scrolling through his phone, playing games that demanded total attention, losing himself in the internet in ways that felt necessary for survival. He had also begun drinking more heavily—a beer or two in the afternoon, sometimes something stronger—and had asked his doctor for sleeping medication, which he took liberally. These strategies quieted the intrusive thoughts temporarily, but they had their own cost. His work had begun to suffer; he'd missed deadlines, made mistakes on installations that he would never have made before. Marcus had grown distant, hurt by Aotea's emotional unavailability and his increasing absences into screens and substances. More troubling still, the avoidance seemed to create a cruel feedback loop: the more hours Aotea spent numbing himself, the more his mind would sharpen its focus on the very things he was trying to escape. When he finally put the phone down or the alcohol wore off, the memories would feel fresher, more intrusive, and his conviction that he was irredeemably flawed—that he deserved what had happened—would deepen, which in turn would make him more hypervigilant, more reactive to any sound or movement, which would drive him back to the screen, the drink, the medication, the endless cycle of avoidance that left him feeling simultaneously trapped and unable to stop.

Aotea arrived at the clinic on a Tuesday morning, pale and exhausted. What had finally pushed him to seek help was a panic attack so severe that he'd collapsed at work, and Marcus's ultimatum: get help or watch him leave. Aotea sat in the waiting room with his hands clenched, certain that no one could help him, convinced that he was broken in ways that therapy couldn't fix, and terrified most of all that if he stopped running from the memories, they would consume him entirely.
